analysis.one_liner: Lets regional groups of states set milk prices above federal minimums to raise dairy farmers' incomes.
analysis.headline: A House Judiciary subcommittee approved the bill 7–3 in July 1999, but the full committee never voted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended, despite 167 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let Northeastern states expand an existing regional dairy compact and let ten Southern states form a new one. Each compact could set a minimum price, above the federal floor, that milk processors must pay dairy farmers for drinking milk. Farmers in the compact regions would get higher, steadier milk prices; the cost would show up in higher retail milk prices for families in those regions.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers in the Northeast and Southern compact states, particularly smaller family farms that sell fluid milk, would earn more per gallon because processors would be required to pay a floor price above the federal minimum. Farm groups and the state delegations that designed the compacts would also gain a permanent regional pricing authority.

how_it_helps.text: The bill renews congressional consent for the Northeast Interstate Dairy Compact and consents to a new Southern Dairy Compact covering ten states, letting those states jointly regulate milk prices across their region.

The compacts can set an 'over-order' minimum price for Class I fluid milk above federal marketing order prices; for the Southern compact the over-order price is capped at $1.50 per gallon at Atlanta, adjusted annually for inflation.
The Southern compact requires a referendum in which at least two-thirds of voting dairy producers must approve any pricing order before it takes effect.

The Southern compact commission must compensate the Commodity Credit Corporation each year for the cost of any surplus milk purchases caused by compact prices, limiting the burden on federal taxpayers.

The compact text requires each state delegation to include at least one working dairy farmer and one consumer representative, and allows reimbursement payments to participants in the WIC nutrition program.

analysis.who_pays: Households in the compact regions would pay more for drinking milk, because processors required to pay the higher floor price pass the cost into retail prices. Dairy farmers outside the compact regions would face compensatory payments on milk they ship into the regulated area, and, under the bill's changes to the Northeast compact, federal taxpayers would lose the compact's requirement to reimburse the Commodity Credit Corporation for surplus dairy purchases triggered by higher compact prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill legally requires milk processors in the regulated area to pay a minimum price above the federal level for fluid milk, a cost that flows through to grocery prices; milk is a larger share of the budget for low-income families.

The bill strikes the existing provision requiring the Northeast Dairy Compact to compensate the Commodity Credit Corporation, so the cost of any federal surplus dairy purchases caused by compact-inflated prices would fall on taxpayers rather than the compact.

The compact's compensatory-payment provisions charge producers outside the region for milk brought into the regulated area, walling regional markets off from outside competition and disadvantaging dairy farmers in states like those in the Midwest.

A price floor on fluid milk can encourage more production of drinking milk than the market wants, which the compact text itself acknowledges by requiring the commission to act to prevent excess local production.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would raise and stabilize incomes for dairy farmers in the Northeast and South, many of them small family operations facing falling milk prices, and it includes real safeguards: a producer referendum, a consumer seat on each delegation, a price cap, and CCC reimbursement in the South. But the funding mechanism is a mandated higher price on a grocery staple, paid by every household that buys milk in the region, and it shields compact-region farmers from outside competition. On balance it is a transfer from milk consumers, spread widely and falling hardest on lower-income families, to a regionally concentrated producer group — with the Northeast portion additionally shifting federal purchase costs back onto taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got a hearing and a subcommittee vote in the House Judiciary Committee in the summer of 1999, but the full committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 28, 1999, and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, which held a hearing on June 17, 1999.
On July 29, 1999, the subcommittee held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee, as amended, by a vote of 7 to 3.
The full Judiciary Committee never voted on the bill, and no House floor vote ever occurred; the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill had 167 cosponsors: 85 Democrats, 81 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Milk drinkers in the Northeast and South and dairy farmers outside the proposed compact regions — particularly in the Midwest — were better off, since they avoided a mandated above-market milk price and new market barriers. Dairy farmers in the compact regions, who had assembled broad bipartisan support, gained nothing.

for.name: Asa Hutchinson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a large bipartisan cosponsor list drawn mostly from Northeastern and Southern dairy states.

for.name: 85 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, mostly from Northeastern and Southern states

for.name: 81 House Republican cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, mostly from Northeastern and Southern dairy states

for.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
for.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction over the bill
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing, then at a July 29, 1999 markup forwarded the bill to the full committee, as amended, by a vote of 7 to 3.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee or scheduled it for a House floor vote after the subcommittee forwarded it; the bill sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: Midwest dairy interests and national milk processors
against.role: Dairy farmer organizations and milk processors outside compact regions
against.what_they_did: Opposed regional dairy compacts, arguing that compact price floors raise retail milk prices and impose compensatory charges on milk shipped into regulated areas from outside.

sides.party_line_note: Support split almost evenly by party — 85 of the 167 cosponsors were Democrats and 81 were Republicans — with the dividing lines running by region (Northeast and South for the bill, Midwest largely against) rather than by party [S4].

industries.industry: Dairy farmers in the Northeast and Southern compact regions
industries.note: The bill guarantees them a minimum price for fluid milk above the federal floor, paid by processors and passed to consumers. Their gain comes directly out of household milk budgets in the regulated states.

industries.industry: Dairy farmers outside the compact regions (especially the Midwest)
industries.note: Compact rules let the commission charge compensatory payments on outside milk brought into the regulated area, walling the regional market off from cheaper suppliers. Outside producers face lower access to nearby urban milk markets.

Handlers must pay the compact over-order price and fund administration through assessments, but they generally pass higher raw-milk costs into retail prices. Consumers, not the processors, absorb most of the final cost.

industries.industry: Federal dairy purchase program (Commodity Credit Corporation)
industries.note: The bill strikes the Northeast compact's requirement to reimburse the Commodity Credit Corporation for surplus purchases caused by compact prices, shifting that potential cost to taxpayers. The new Southern compact keeps a reimbursement requirement.
